rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here tadʿūna means that the polytheists worship the idols.
rows.anchor: «تدعون» تعبدون

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative takes it to mean that they call the idols gods.
rows.anchor: وقيل: تدعونها آلهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min dūni Allāh means other than God.
rows.anchor: «من دون الله» أي من غير الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idols are called servants because they are owned by God and subjected to Him.
rows.anchor: وسميت الأوثان عبادا لأنها مملوكة لله مسخرة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the idols are created beings like you.
rows.anchor: الحسن: المعنى أن الأصنام مخلوقة أمثالكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masculine wording treats idols as people because polytheists thought they could harm and benefit like people.
rows.anchor: ولما اعتقد المشركون أن الأصنام تضر وتنفع أجراها مجرى الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge is to ask the idols for benefit or harm.
rows.anchor: ومعنى «فادعوهم» أي فاطلبوا منهم النفع والضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge tests their claim that worshipping idols brings benefit.
rows.anchor: إن عبادة الأصنام تنفع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the command means worship them.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: معنى فادعوهم فاعبدوهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God rebukes them: people are superior to idols, so it is foolish to worship them; an object of worship ought to possess bodily faculties.
rows.anchor: أي أنتم أفضل منهم فكيف تعبدونهم. والغرض بيان جهلهم

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reads inna lightly with kasra and reads ʿibādan and amthālakum in the accusative.
rows.anchor: قرأ سعيد بن جبير: «إن الذين تدعون من دون الله عبادا أمثالكم»

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: On Saʿīd ibn Jubayr’s reading, idols are stone and wood, so people worship what is nobler than themselves.
rows.anchor: أي هي حجارة وخشب فأنتم تعبدون ما أنتم أشرف منه

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Naḥḥās rejects this reading: it conflicts with the codex; Sibawayh favors a nominative predicate after inna used as mā; al-Kisāʾī says inna rarely means mā without an affirmative.
rows.anchor: قال النحاس: وهذه قراءة لا ينبغي أن يقرأ بها من ثلاث جهات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in fal-yastajībū is originally kasra, omitted because it is heavy.
rows.anchor: الأصل أن تكون اللام مكسورة، فحذفت الكسرة لثقلها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An ellipsis means: invite them to follow you and let them respond if you are right that they are gods.
rows.anchor: في الكلام حذف، المعنى: فادعوهم إلى أن يتبعوكم

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وشيبة
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar and Shaybah read yabṭishūna with a ḍamma on ṭāʾ; this is a dialect form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر وشيبة { أم لهم أيد يبطشون بها } بضم الطاء، وهي لغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hand, foot, and ear are feminine nouns and take tāʾ in diminutives; yad adds yāʾ in the diminutive to restore its root, yielding yadiyyah with doubled yāʾ.
rows.anchor: واليد والرجل والأذن مؤنثات يصغرن بالهاء. وتزاد في اليد ياء في التصغير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The partners whom the audience is told to summon are the idols.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { قل ادعوا شركآءكم } أي الأصنام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge is directed to the people together with their idols.
rows.anchor: { ثم كيدون } أنتم وهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fa-lā tunẓirūn means do not delay or give respite.
rows.anchor: { فلا تنظرون } أي فلا تؤخرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The original forms are kaydūnī and tunẓirūnī; the yāʾ is omitted because the kasra signals it.
rows.anchor: والأصل «كيدوني» حذفت الياء لأن الكسرة تدل عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kayd means scheming and can also mean war; Arabs say a raider went out and met no fighting.
rows.anchor: والكيد المكر. والكيد الحرب يقال: غزا فلم يلق كيدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God protects and supports the speaker; a walī guards and prevents harm.
rows.anchor: أي الذي يتولى نصري وحفظي الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A walī is one who guards something and prevents harm from reaching it.
rows.anchor: وولي الشيء: الذي يحفظه ويمنع عنه الضرر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book mentioned here is the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: والكتاب: القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s taking charge of the righteous means that He preserves them.
rows.anchor: { وهو يتولى الصالحين } أي يحفظهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels are unanimously identified as those near their Lord.
rows.anchor: يعني الملائكة بإجماع

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj explains nearness to God as nearness to His mercy; anyone near His mercy is described as with Him.
rows.anchor: كل قريب من رحمة الله عز وجل فهو عنده عن الزجاج

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another explanation says the angels are with God because they are in a place reached only by His decree.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: لأنهم في موضع لا ينفذ فيه إلا حكم الله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation describes the angels as God’s messengers, like saying a king has many troops at his court.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لأنهم رسل الله كما يقال: عند الخليفة جيش كثير

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view makes this nearness honorific: it denotes rank, not physical distance.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هذا على جهة التشريف لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels glorify God by exalting Him and declaring Him free of every evil.
rows.anchor: ويعظمونه وينزهونه عن كل سوء

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One interpretation takes their prostration to mean that they pray.
rows.anchor: قيل: يصلون

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interprets prostration as humble submission, unlike the behavior of sinners.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يذلون، خلاف أهل المعاصي

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority hold that this verse is a place where a Qurʾān reciter performs the prostration of recitation.
rows.anchor: والجمهور من العلماء في أن هذا موضع سجود للقارىء

rows.speaker: ابن حبيب وابن وهب وإسحاق
rows.claim: One count gives fifteen prostrations, from the end of al-Aʿrāf through the end of al-ʿAlaq; this is Ibn Ḥabīb, one report from Ibn Wahb, and Isḥāq’s view.
rows.anchor: وهو قول ابن حبيب وابن وهب في رواية وإسحاق

rows.speaker: بعض العلماء
rows.claim: Some add the prostration at 15:98, making sixteen.
rows.anchor: ومن العلماء من زاد سجدة الحجر قوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: ابن وهب
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Wahb counts fourteen, omitting the second al-Ḥajj prostration; this is the Ḥanafī position.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أربع عشرة قاله ابن وهب في الرواية الأخرى عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī considers omitting the second al-Ḥajj prostration correct because the report establishing it is not sound.
rows.anchor: والصحيح سقوطها لأن الحديث لم يصح بثبوتها

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن منين
rows.claim: A report to ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ says the Prophet taught fifteen prostrations, including three in al-Mufaṣṣal and two in al-Ḥajj; ʿAbd al-Ḥaqq says Ibn Munayn is not a reliable proof.
rows.anchor: ورواه ابن ماجه وأبو داود في سننهما عن عبد الله بن منين من بني عبد كلال

rows.speaker: عقبة بن عامر
rows.claim: Abū Dāwūd reports ʿUqbah ibn ʿĀmir asking whether al-Ḥajj has two prostrations; the Prophet says yes, but Ibn Lahīʿah in its chain is very weak.
rows.anchor: عقبة بن عامر قال قلت: يا رسول الله، أفي سورة الحج سجدتان

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī counts both al-Ḥajj prostrations and omits the prostration in Ṣād.
rows.anchor: وأثبتهما الشافعي وأسقط سجدة ص

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: The famous Mālikī count is eleven, omitting the last al-Ḥajj prostration and three in al-Mufaṣṣal; it is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: وهو مشهور مذهب مالك. وروي عن ابن عباس وابن عمر وغيرهما

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: Ibn Mājah reports Abū al-Dardāʾ saying he prostrated with the Prophet eleven times, listing al-Aʿrāf, al-Raʿd, al-Naḥl, Banī Isrāʾīl, Maryam, one in al-Ḥajj, al-Furqān, al-Naml, al-Sajdah, Ṣād, and one of the Ḥawāmīm.
rows.anchor: وفي سنن ابن ماجه عن أبي الدرداء قال: سجدت مع النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إحدى عشرة سجدة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another count attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās is ten, omitting the last al-Ḥajj prostration, Ṣād, and the three in al-Mufaṣṣal.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عشر، وأسقط آخرة الحج وص وثلاث المفصل ذكر عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further count is four: al-Sajdah, Ḥā Mīm al-Sajdah, al-Najm, and al-ʿAlaq.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنها أربع، سجدة آلم تنزيل وحم تنزيل والنجم والعلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Counts differ because reports and practice vary, and scholars disagree whether Qurʾānic commands to prostrate mean recitation prostration or required prayer prostration.
rows.anchor: وسبب الخلاف اختلاف النقل في الأحاديث والعمل

rows.speaker: مالك والشافعي
rows.claim: Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī hold that prostration of recitation is not obligatory.
rows.anchor: فقال مالك والشافعي: ليس بواجب

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfah holds recitation prostration obligatory, citing the unqualified command, reports about Satan weeping when Adam’s child prostrates and about Paradise and Hell, and the Prophet’s practice.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة: هو واجب. وتعلق بأن مطلق الأمر بالسجود على الوجوب

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī relies on the sound report that ʿUmar prostrated after reciting a sajdah, then later said God had not made it obligatory unless people chose.
rows.anchor: حديث عمر الثابت خرجه البخاري أنه قرأ آية سجدة على المنبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿUmar’s statement before the Companions, without objection, establishes consensus that recitation prostration is not obligatory.
rows.anchor: فلم ينكر عليه أحد فثبت الإجماع به في ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report that Adam’s child was commanded to prostrate refers to an obligatory prostration; the Prophet’s regular practice indicates recommendation.
rows.anchor: فإخبار عن السجود الواجب. ومواظبة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم تدل على الاستحباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Recitation prostration requires prayer’s conditions: purity, intention, qibla, and a permissible time; Ibn ʿUmar and al-Shaʿbī are reported to allow it without purity.
rows.anchor: ولا خلاف في أن سجود القرآن يحتاج إلى ما تحتاج إليه الصلاة من طهارة حدث ونجس

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Al-Bukhārī reports Ibn ʿUmar prostrating without purity; Ibn al-Mundhir reports the same of al-Shaʿbī.
rows.anchor: ذكر البخاري عن ابن عمر أنه كان يسجد على غير طهارة

rows.speaker: الشافعي وأحمد وإسحاق
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, and Isḥāq require takbīr and raising the hands for prostration.
rows.anchor: فذهب الشافعي وأحمد وإسحاق إلى أنه يكبر ويرفع للتكبير لها

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿUmar says the Prophet said takbīr when prostrating and rising.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عمر أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كان إذا سجد كبر

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik’s well-known position is takbīr on lowering and rising inside prayer; views differ on takbīr outside prayer, though most jurists require it.
rows.anchor: مشهور مذهب مالك أنه يكبر لها في الخفض والرفع في الصلاة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority do not require salām after recitation prostration, while a group of early authorities and Isḥāq require it.
rows.anchor: ولا سلام لها عند الجمهور. وذهب جماعة من السلف وإسحاق إلى أنه يسلم منها

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī prefers requiring salām: an act with takbīr should have an exit like prayer; this is even more fitting than for funeral prayer.
rows.anchor: وهذه عبادة لها تكبير، فكان لها تحليل كصلاة الجنازة بل أولى، لأنها فعل وصلاة الجنازة قول. وهذا اختيار ابن العربي

rows.speaker: الشافعي وجماعة
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī and a group allow prostration at any time because it is prayer for a specific cause.
rows.anchor: يسجد في سائر الأوقات مطلقا لأنها صلاة لسبب. وهو قول الشافعي وجماعة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view permits prostration until dawn brightens or until the sun yellows after ʿAṣr.
rows.anchor: ما لم يسفر الصبح، أو ما لم تصفر الشمس بعد العصر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view forbids prostration after both dawn and ʿAṣr.
rows.anchor: لا يسجد بعد الصبح ولا بعد العصر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view allows it after dawn but not after ʿAṣr; these positions occur in the Mālikī school.
rows.anchor: يسجد بعد الصبح ولا يسجد بعد العصر. وهذه الثلاثة الأقوال في مذهبنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Timing opinions balance recitation prostration against the general ban on prayer after ʿAṣr and dawn, and differ on that ban’s rationale.
rows.anchor: سبب الخلاف معارضة ما يقتضيه سبب قراءة السجدة من السجود المرتب عليها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās transmits from the Prophet a supplication asking God to remove a burden, record reward, and store it as a treasure.
rows.anchor: رواه ابن عباس عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ذكره ابن ماجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In voluntary prayer, prostrate alone or in a congregation when disruption is not feared; the stated ruling permits prostration even if feared, though another view forbids that.
rows.anchor: فإن كان في نافلة سجد إن كان منفردا أو في جماعة وأمن التخليط فيها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A view says not to prostrate in voluntary congregational prayer when it may confuse the congregation.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لا يسجد

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik’s well-known position forbids recitation prostration in obligatory prayer, whether quiet or aloud and alone or in a congregation, as an extra prostration.
rows.anchor: المشهور عن مالك النهي عنه فيها، سواء كانت صلاة سر أو جهر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation is fear of confusing the congregation; on this rationale it is allowed alone or where confusion is unlikely.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معلل بخوف التخليط على الجماعة وهذا أشبه

rows.speaker: أبو رافع
rows.claim: Al-Bukhārī alone reports Abū Rāfiʿ praying ʿIshāʾ with Abū Hurayrah, who prostrated at al-Inshiqāq and said he had done so behind the Prophet and would continue until meeting him.
rows.anchor: روى البخاري عن أبي رافع قال: صليت مع أبي هريرة العتمة، فقرأ

rows.speaker: عمران بن حصين
rows.claim: ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn’s answer about a person who hears a prostration but was not seated for it implies the listener is not obliged to prostrate.
rows.anchor: وقيل لعمران بن حصين: الرجل يسمع السجدة ولم يجلس لها

rows.speaker: سلمان
rows.claim: Salmān said, “We did not come for this,” regarding recitation prostration.
rows.anchor: وقال سلمان: ما لهذا غدونا

rows.speaker: عثمان
rows.claim: ʿUthmān held that prostration is due only from someone who listens attentively.
rows.anchor: وقال عثمان: إنما السجدة على من استمعها

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhrī requires purity; at home face the qibla, while a mounted traveler may face any direction.
rows.anchor: وقال الزهري: لا يسجد إلا أن يكون طاهرا

rows.speaker: السائب
rows.claim: Al-Sāʾib did not prostrate when a preacher prostrated.
rows.anchor: وكان السائب لا يسجد لسجود القاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet must convey this meaning to the disbelievers, in these words or another phrasing.
rows.anchor: أمر النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أن يقول للكفار هذا المعنى، وسواء قاله بهذه العبارة أو غيرها

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah discusses al-Kisāʾī’s report that Ibn Masʿūd’s codex reads “if they cease”; on that wording the message would depend on those exact words.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ولو كان كما ذكر الكسائي أنه في مصحف عبد الله بن مسعود

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah says “if they desist” means desisting from disbelief, as the conditional answer promises forgiveness for what came before.
rows.anchor: يريد عن الكفر. قال ابن عطية: ولا بد والحامل على ذلك جواب الشرط

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد أحمد بن محمد الزبيري
rows.claim: Abū Saʿīd al-Zubayrī’s verse says that confessing and stopping wrongdoing merits pardon.
rows.anchor: ولقد أحسن القائل أبو سعيد أحمد بن محمد الزبيري

rows.speaker: عمرو بن العاص
rows.claim: Muslim reports Abū Shumāsah al-Muḥāribī visiting the dying ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, who recalls the Prophet saying Islam, emigration, and pilgrimage each efface what came before.
rows.anchor: روى مسلم عن أبي شماسة المهري قال: حضرنا عمرو بن العاص

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī calls the pardon divine kindness: wiping away prior sins makes repentance and conversion easier, since fear would deter people from returning to Islam.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي: هذه لطيفة من الله سبحانه من بها على الخلق

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī warns that deterring repentance harms people, while easing the way to mercy benefits them.
rows.anchor: فالتنفير مفسدة للخليقة، والتيسير مصلحة لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim report tells of a man who killed ninety-nine people, was told by an ascetic he had no repentance, killed him too, and reached one hundred; despair drove him to kill.
rows.anchor: لا توبة لك فقتله فكمل به مائة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reportedly told a would-be killer there was no repentance to deter him, but assured an actual killer of repentance to draw him toward it.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما أنه كان إذا جاء إليه رجل لم يقتل

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik, transmitted by Ibn al-Qāsim and Ibn Wahb, says pre-Islamic divorce and oaths lapse on conversion, but a convert remains liable for slandering or stealing from a Muslim.
rows.anchor: قال ابن القاسم وابن وهب عن مالك فيمن طلق في الشرك ثم أسلم فلا طلاق له

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Ashhab transmits Mālik limiting pardon to pre-Islamic matters, including property and blood claims.
rows.anchor: وروى أشهب عن مالك أنه قال: إنما يعني الله عز وجل ما قد مضى قبل الإسلام

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī considers the broad pardon correct, given the verse’s general wording, the report that Islam erases what preceded it, and the benefit of easing conversion.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي: وهذا هو الصواب لما قدمناه من عموم قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Combatant disbelievers’ offenses in enemy territory are forgiven; safe-conduct visitors and dhimmīs retain penalties for slander, theft, and murder because the covenant was breached.
rows.anchor: أما الكافر الحربي فلا خلاف في إسقاط ما فعله في حال كفره

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī in Iraq held that a Christian who committed adultery then converted is not flogged or banished; Ibn al-Mundhir says this agrees with what is reported from Mālik.
rows.anchor: عن الشافعي رضي الله عنه إذ هو بالعراق لا حد عليه ولا تغريب

rows.speaker: أبو ثور
rows.claim: Abū Thawr says a convert who admits while Muslim that he committed adultery as a Christian receives the penalty.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو ثور: إذا أقر وهو مسلم أنه زنى وهو كافر أقيم عليه الحد

rows.speaker: الكوفي
rows.claim: The Kūfan authority disagrees with Abū Thawr and says the convert is not punished for that adultery.
rows.anchor: وحكي عن الكوفي أنه قال: لا يحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view treats a returning apostate like an original disbeliever who converts, imposing no liability for missed prayers, offenses, or destroyed property during apostasy.
rows.anchor: فقيل: حكمه حكم الكافر الأصلي إذا أسلم لا يؤخذ بشيء مما أحدثه في حال ارتداده

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: In one opinion al-Shāfiʿī makes a returning apostate liable for all rights of God and people, reasoning that if human rights remain, divine rights should too.
rows.anchor: وقال الشافعي في أحد قوليه: يلزمه كل حق لله عز وجل وللآدمي

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfah says rights owed to God lapse for a returning apostate, but rights owed to people remain.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة: ما كان لله يسقط، وما كان للآدمي لا يسقط

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī endorses the Ḥanafī view: God does not need His due, people do; children likewise owe no divine duties but remain subject to human claims.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي: وهو قول علمائنا لأن الله تعالى مستغن عن حقه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The verse’s promise is also cited as general for rights owed to God.
rows.anchor: قالوا: وقوله تعالى { قل للذين كفروا إن ينتهوا يغفر لهم ما قد سلف } عام في الحقوق لله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “If they return” means return to fighting: the unqualified ʿāda denotes returning to a prior state, and disbelievers had not left disbelief.
rows.anchor: الخامسة: قوله تعالى: { وإن يعودوا } يريد إلى القتال

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah says fighting is the only prior state they could return to, not disbelief, which they never abandoned.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ولسنا نجد في هذه الآية لهؤلاء الكفار حالة تشبه ما ذكرنا إلا القتال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic ʿāda can mean “became” when followed by a predicate, as in ʿāda Zaydun malikan; this does not imply return to an earlier state.
rows.anchor: لأنها قد تجيء في كلام العرب داخلة في الابتداء والخبر، فيكون معناها معنى صار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Umayyah ibn Abī al-Ṣalt’s cited line illustrates ʿāda meaning “became,” not “returned,” because the verb is restricted by its predicate.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول أمية بن أبي الصلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Umayyah’s poetic line about bowls of milk mixed with water that became urine witnesses ʿāda in the sense “became.”
rows.anchor: تلك المكارم لا قعبان من لبن شيبا بماء فعادا بعد أبوالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The former peoples’ precedent combines warning and threat with examples of nations destroyed by God’s punishment.
rows.anchor: عبارة تجمع الوعيد والتهديد والتمثيل بمن هلك من الأمم في سالف الدهر بعذاب الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase begins a nominal sentence; baʿḍuhum may begin a second sentence or be a substitute, with min baʿḍ as predicate.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { المنافقون والمنافقات } ابتداء. { بعضهم } ابتداء ثان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites are like one thing in their departure from religion.
rows.anchor: ومعنى { بعضهم من بعض } أي هم كالشيء الواحد في الخروج عن الدين

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj connects this to hypocrites claiming they belong to believers but do not; they resemble one another in enjoining wrong and forbidding right.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج، هذا متصل بقوله: «يحلفون بالله إنهم لمنكم وما هم منكم»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Withholding their hands refers to abandoning jihad and failing to fulfill what is due.
rows.anchor: وقبض أيديهم عبارة عن ترك الجهاد، وفيما يجب عليهم من حق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Forgetting” means neglect: they neglected God’s commands, so He left them in doubt.
rows.anchor: والنسيان: الترك هنا أي تركوا ما أمرهم الله به فتركهم في الشك

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says they neglected God’s command until it seemed forgotten, so God treated them as forgotten with respect to reward.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنهم تركوا أمره حتى صار كالمنسي فصيرهم بمنزلة المنسي من ثوابه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatādah says God has forgotten them with respect to good, but not evil.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: «نسيهم» أي من الخير فأما من الشر فلم ينسهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fisq is departure from obedience and religion.
rows.anchor: والفسق: الخروج عن الطاعة والدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believing men and women are allies because their hearts are united in affection, love, and compassion.
rows.anchor: أي قلوبهم متحدة في التواد والتحاب والتعاطف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike believers, hypocrites are “of one another” because their hearts differ and they are only grouped together in judgment.
rows.anchor: وقال في المنافقين «بعضهم من بعض» لأن قلوبهم مختلفة ولكن يضم بعضهم إلى بعض في الحكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Enjoining right means worshipping and affirming God’s oneness, and what follows from that.
rows.anchor: أي بعبادة الله تعالى وتوحيده، وكل ما أتبع ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forbidding wrong means prohibiting worship of idols and what follows from that.
rows.anchor: عن عبادة الأوثان وكل ما أتبع ذلك

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī transmits from Abū al-ʿĀliyah that Qurʾānic mentions of enjoining right and forbidding wrong mean forbidding worship of idols and devils.
rows.anchor: وذكر الطبري عن أبي العالية أنه قال: كل ما ذكر الله في القرآن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says prayer here means the five prescribed prayers, making zakāt the obligatory alms.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: هي الصلوات الخمس، وبحسب هذا تكون الزكاة هنا المفروضة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah says praise for voluntary prayers is more emphatic, since one who establishes them is more likely to establish obligations.
rows.anchor: ابن عطية: والمدح عندي بالنوافل أبلغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Obedience to God concerns obligations, and obedience to the Messenger concerns what he prescribed for them.
rows.anchor: في الفرائض { ورسوله } فيما سن لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The future sīn delays the promised mercy in expression so souls can savor anticipation of God’s favor, which He guarantees to fulfill.
rows.anchor: والسين في قوله: { سيرحمهم الله } مدخلة في الوعد مهلة لتكون النفوس تتنعم برجائه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatādah says an Anṣārī pledged charity if God granted him wealth; when granted it, he broke his pledge, illustrating that lying leads to wickedness.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: هذا رجل من الأنصار قال: لئن رزقني الله شيئا لأؤدين فيه حقه

rows.speaker: أبو أمامة الباهلي
rows.claim: Abū Umāmah’s report says Thaʿlabah sought wealth despite the Prophet’s warning that little one can thank is better than much one cannot bear; his sheep multiplied, drew him from congregational prayer, and he refused collectors, calling alms the sister of jizya. The account is called famous.
rows.anchor: وروى علي بن يزيد عن القاسم عن أبي أمامة الباهلي

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another account says Thaʿlabah became wealthy by inheriting from a paternal cousin.
rows.anchor: وقيل: سبب غناء ثعلبة أنه ورث ابن عم له

rows.speaker: ابن عبد البر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr says it is said that Thaʿlabah ibn Ḥāṭib was the one in the verse who withheld zakāt.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عبد البر: قيل إن ثعلبة بن حاطب هو الذي نزل فيه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās gives another occasion: Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿah swore to give charity and support relatives when delayed Syrian funds arrived, then became miserly.
rows.anchor: وذكر عن ابن عباس في سبب نزول الآية أن حاطب بن أبي بلتعة أبطأ عنه ماله بالشام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī rejects blaming Thaʿlabah: he was a Badr veteran and Anṣārī whose faith God and Messenger attested, so reports against him are unsound.
rows.anchor: قلت: وثعلبة بدري أنصاري وممن شهد الله له ورسوله بالإيمان

rows.speaker: أبو عمر
rows.claim: Abū ʿUmar cautions that identifying Thaʿlabah as the zakāt refuser in whom the verse was revealed may be incorrect.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عمر: ولعل قول من قال في ثعلبة أنه مانع الزكاة

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the verse was revealed about hypocrites Natil ibn al-Ḥārith, Jadd ibn Qays, and Muʿattib ibn Qushayr.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: إن الآية نزلت في رجال من المنافقين نبتل بن الحارث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī finds al-Ḍaḥḥāk’s account more plausible, but “caused hypocrisy to follow” implies the vow-taker was not already a hypocrite unless it means his hypocrisy increased until death.
rows.anchor: قلت: وهذا أشبه بنزول الآية فيهم إلا أن قوله { فأعقبهم نفاقا } يدل على أن الذي عاهد الله لم يكن منافقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this account the Prophet says mountains could move with him as gold if he wished; Thaʿlabah again seeks wealth and pledges charity.
rows.anchor: أما ترضى أن تكون مثل نبي الله لو شئت أن تسير معي الجبال ذهبا لسارت

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet sends two collectors to Thaʿlabah and a man of Banū Sulaym after the charity command; Thaʿlabah refuses, calling alms the sister of jizya.
rows.anchor: فبعث صلى الله عليه وسلم رجلين على الصدقة، وقال لهما: «مرا بثعلبة وبفلان

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says God overlooks what the Prophet’s community inwardly whispers unless they say or enact it.
rows.anchor: تجاوز الله لأمتي عما وسوست به نفوسها ما لم ينطق به لسان أو تعمله يد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the promise was a vow, fulfillment is obligatory and abandonment sinful; if an oath, fulfillment is not obligatory by agreement.
rows.anchor: إن كان نذرا فالوفاء بالنذر واجب من غير خلاف وتركه معصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that a poor person asked for wealth not yet subject to zakāt, intending to perform its due, then withheld what he undertook; seeking wealth for duties entangled him through impure intention or adverse decree.
rows.anchor: فلما آتاه الله ما شاء من ذلك ترك ما التزم مما كان يلزمه في أصل الدين

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet advises considering a wish because its unseen outcome may tempt or overwhelm and cause ruin; religious and afterlife aspirations are praiseworthy.
rows.anchor: إذا تمنى أحدكم فلينظر ما يتمنى فإنه لا يدري ما كتب له في غيب الله عز وجل

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfah holds that saying “if I own this, it is charity” makes the gift binding.
rows.anchor: وبه قال أبو حنيفة

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī says a conditional gift does not bind; he holds the same on conditional divorce and emancipation.
rows.anchor: وقال الشافعي: لا يلزمه والخلاف في الطلاق مثله، وكذلك في العتق

rows.speaker: أحمد بن حنبل
rows.claim: Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal makes conditional emancipation binding as a devotional act attached by vow, but not divorce, a disposition on a specific object that cannot attach to liability.
rows.anchor: وقال أحمد بن حنبل: يلزمه ذلك في العتق ولا يلزمه في الطلاق

rows.speaker: عمرو بن شعيب
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī cites ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb’s report from his father and grandfather: no vow, emancipation, or divorce applies to what one does not own; al-Tirmidhī calls it hasan and the best on this topic.
rows.anchor: عن عمرو بن شعيب عن أبيه عن جده قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī says al-Shāfiʿī’s followers list many reports on this issue, but none is sound, leaving only the verse’s apparent wording.
rows.anchor: ابن العربي: وسرد أصحاب الشافعي في هذا الباب أحاديث كثيرة لم يصح منها شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ātāhum min faḍlihi means God gave them from His bounty.
rows.anchor: أي أعطاهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their miserliness means withholding charity, spending on good, and fulfilling what they promised and undertook.
rows.anchor: أي بإعطاء الصدقة وبإنفاق المال في الخير، وبالوفاء بما ضمنوا والتزموا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tawallaw means turning away from obedience to God.
rows.anchor: { وتولوا } أي عن طاعة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They openly turned away from Islam.
rows.anchor: أي عن الإسلام، أي مظهرون للإعراض عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb has two objects; God is its implied subject, causing hypocrisy to follow for them.
rows.anchor: مفعولان أي أعقبهم الله تعالى نفاقا في قلوبهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative makes their miserliness the subject that caused hypocrisy, matching the statement that they were miserly.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أي أعقبهم البخل نفاقا ولهذا قال: «بخلوا به»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase is genitive and may mean that they meet their miserliness, or its requital, as one says that tomorrow you meet your deeds.
rows.anchor: في موضع خفض أي يلقون بخلهم، أي جزاء بخلهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view is that they meet God; this implies that the person died a hypocrite.
rows.anchor: وقيل: { إلى يوم يلقونه } أي يلقون الله. وفي هذا دليل على أنه مات منافقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This inference makes Thaʿlabah or Ḥāṭib unlikely as the subject of revelation; the supporting report is cut off after its introduction.
rows.anchor: وهو يبعد أن يكون المنزل فيه ثعلبة أو حاطب لأن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال لعمر
